newsitem.title: GERMANY: German leaders firmly against costly EU job deal.
newsitem.headline: German leaders firmly against costly EU job deal.

text.p: German leaders said on Sunday they were unalterably opposed to French calls for a costly drive to create jobs for Europe's unemployed but were confident a face-saving agreement for more coordination was within reach.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's top deputy Wolfgang Schaeuble all dismissed the French ideas as obsolete and said there was no chance Germany would accept them at the European Union's summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday.
"We have been working on this for days," Waigel said. "We will try today and continue tomorrow morning. I am cautiously optimistic. But we have quite a bit still to take care of."

He said Germany would remain firm on insisting that there would be no funding for additional job-creation programmes. He said France also had no interest in creating new bureaucracies and deficit-spending schemes to spur job creation.

"Employment policies have to remain the responsibility of the states. We have to see that we reach a reasonable result. The stability pact cannot be undermined or affected in any way. Not a single comma or decimal point can be changed."
The summit, called to agree a new EU treaty, has been overshadowed by the rift between France and Germany over how to proceed toward monetary union.

EU countries hoped the summit would ratify a German-designed stability pact intended to impose discipline for the proposed single European currency by punishing nations failing to adhere to strict fiscal standards.
But France's new Socialist prime minister Lionel Jospin upset the plans by demanding last week that the 18 million jobless people in the EU be taken into account.

Kohl, who met French leaders on Friday in a fruitless bid to reach agreement, ran into a stormy protest by 2,700 farmers who gathered outside an official ceremony in the Bavarian town of Bad Woerishofen on Sunday with banners reading "Farm Killer" and "Helmut Kohl Is To Germany What Mad Cow Disease Is To England".
"We are doing everything humanly possible in Brussels," Kohl told them. "A society without farmers would be a poor society."

Schaeuble, leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats in parliament, said most EU nations were on Germany's side in the dispute. Raising taxes and debt to finance jobs schemes, he said, had failed in the past and wouldn't work in the future.

"The problem of unemployment cannot be resolved with higher taxes or higher borrowing," Schaeuble told the newsmagazine Der Spiegel. "Deficit-spending to create new jobs and boost the economy is an obsolete economic theory."

But Gerhard Schroeder, a leading figure in Germany's opposition Social Democrats and likely challenger to Kohl in next year's elections, said he supported France's efforts to create more jobs in the EU with an employment programme.

"It is important that the employment chapter be filled with content and funding," said Schroeder, the premier of Lower Saxony state, in an interview with the Handelsblatt newspaper to be published on Monday.
"The federal government has been blocking this project long enough," Schroeder added.
Kinkel, in an interview with Welt am Sonntag newspaper, said there would be a chapter in the Amsterdam treaty on employment but there would not be any new spending for it.
"There will be no transfer from Germany of additional authorities to the EU and no additional funding," Kinkel said.
Edmund Stoiber, a leading conservative and well-known euro-sceptic, turned up the volume, saying the euro single currency must be delayed if stability targets are not met.
Politicians will lose public confidence if they trade the mark for a weaker currency.
The Bavarian premier said in an interview with Bild am Sonntag newspaper that replacing the mark with a weaker single European currency could harm German democracy.
"The overriding question for politicians and especially for the public at large is not when the euro will be introduced but rather whether it is a stable euro," Stoiber said.

"And anyone who would replace the strong mark with a weaker euro and thus turn the currency conversion into a currency reform would destroy the public's confidence in politicians and damage democracy in Germany."

Stoiber's remarks came as a Forsa research institute survey found a slim majority of Germans against the euro. The survey of 1,011 Germans showed 51 percent opposed the euro's introduction while 34 percent were in favour.
The Bundesbank denied a report in Der Spiegel claiming central bank president Hans Tietmeyer had urged the creation of a plan to ensure an orderly delay in monetary union.
